chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Jarud, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

There is no soul that is killed — righteous or immoral — except that it will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection clinging to its killer, its (own severed) head in his right hand and its jugular veins streaming with blood, saying: 'O Lord! Ask this one why he killed me.'

So if it was killed in obedience to God, the killer will be rewarded with Paradise and the killed one will be taken to the Fire; but if he says it was in obedience to so-and-so (other than God), it will be said to him: 'Kill him just as he killed you.' Then God, Mighty and Majestic, will deal with both of them afterwards as He wills.

key_terms.طَاعَةِ اللَّهِ: Obedience to God — the only legitimate justification for killing in this context (e.g., divinely sanctioned jihad)
key_terms.فُلَان: So-and-so — euphemism for unlawful worldly authority, contrasted with divine authority
key_terms.مَشِيئَة: Divine will — God's absolute discretion over final outcomes after the retributive process
key_terms.نَفْس: Soul/person — used here to emphasize the sanctity of every human life, righteous or sinful
key_terms.يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ: Day of Resurrection — the eschatological moment when all deeds are reckoned

ai.seo_question: What happens to a murdered soul on the Day of Resurrection according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) describes a vivid eschatological scene on the Day of Resurrection: every murdered soul — whether righteous or sinful — will confront its killer in a dramatic public reckoning. The slain will hold their own severed head in one hand and grip their killer by the other, their blood still flowing, demanding divine judgment. The outcome depends entirely on the motive for the killing: if for God's cause, the killer is rewarded and the killed condemned; if for worldly allegiances, the killed soul receives retributive justice. God retains ultimate discretion over both parties. This hadith establishes the absolute gravity of taking a life and the certainty of eschatological accountability, regardless of the victim's moral status.
